Endoscopy is recommended for patients with alarm symptoms, onset over age 50, or prolonged severe symptoms. B

Antisecretory therapy is the mainstay of pharmacotherapy for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) providing the most rapid symptomatic relief and healing of esophagitis in the highest percentage of patients. There is no difference between PPIs regarding therapeutic efficacy. A
Although less effective than PPIs, histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs) given in divided doses will provide symptomatic relief in patients with less severe symptoms of GERD. A
Vonoprazan may be superior to lansoprazole for treatment of severe erosive esophagitis but not for non-erosive GERD. B
After an initial course of treatment, on-demand (patient-directed therapy) is a clinically and cost-effective means to provide symptomatic relief from uncomplicated GERD. B

Eosinophilic esophagitis: suspect in younger, white, male patients, if food bolus obstruction, or seasonal variation; diagnose with biopsy showing eosinophilic invasion; treat with PPI bid, topical/inhaled steroids, food elimination, and possibly dupilumab.B

background.definition: The term GERD is used to describe the symptoms and changes of the esophageal mucosa that result from reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus. The classic defining symptoms of heartburn and acid regurgitation may or may not be present during this condition. Erosive esophagitis is more severe and is characterized by esophageal sores and ulcers. Eosinophilic esophagitis is a subtype triggered by antigen exposure to the esophagus and an inflammatory cascade.

list.listitem: Roughly 5 per 1000 person-years in the UK and US populations and 0.84 in pediatric age range 1 to 17 in the UK.

Prevalence varies from 18% to 28% in North America, 9% to 33% in the Middle East, 9% to 26% in Europe, 23% in South America, 12% in Australia and 3% to 8% in East Asia. It is prevalent worldwide and the disease burden may be increasing.
44% of US adults have symptoms monthly, 14% weekly, 7% daily.
Eosinophilic esophagitis: 5 to 20 new cases per 100,000 in Europe and North America.
GERD is the most common GI related diagnosis given in USA office visits.
Two of the top five selling drugs in the USA are PPIs.
Studies assessing health-related quality of life report that patients with GERD have worse emotional wellbeing scores than patients with hypertension and diabetes mellitus.

GERD and erosive esophagitis: acid reflux is central, and is associated with transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations, weakened esophageal sphincter tone, hiatal hernia, and delayed gastric emptying and impaired esophageal peristalsis.
Eosinophilic esophagitis: there is a genetic component and it appears to be triggered by food or environmental antigen exposure, followed by an inflammatory cascade.
No gold standard diagnostic test exists for the diagnosis of GERD. C
Classic symptoms of heartburn and acid regurgitation are specific enough to establish a diagnosis but their absence does not rule out GERD (see ). B
Although pH probe is accepted as the standard for research purposes, false positives and false negatives may occur. B
Endoscopy is recommended for patients with alarm symptoms, onset over age 50, or prolonged severe symptoms. B
Suspect eosinophilic esophagitis (EE) in patients with difficulty swallowing food or saliva, recurrent choking, belching or regurgitation, and other obstructive symptoms.

Differential.Differential_Features: Episodic epigastric pain, often nausea, heartburn, regurgitation
As above, with no definable etiology. Acid exposure is quantifiably normal and perceived symptoms are unrelated to reflux events.
Epigastric pain often relieved by eating, opposite of GERD
Gallstones produce right upper quadrant abdominal pain and dyspepsia with temporal relation to ingestion of a high-fat meal
Mucosal injury to gastric lining and esophagus due to medication (NSAIDs, aspirin)
Radiating substernal chest pressure similar in presentation to and often mistaken for GERD
Epigastric abdominal pain, may radiate to back, associated with nausea and vomiting
Heartburn, regurgitation, vomiting, food bolus obstruction, dysphagia. More common in white race, men, and earlier in life.

list.listitem: Classic symptoms of burning in the chest, with a sour or bitter taste, and acid regurgitation have been shown to identify GERD correctly with a sensitivity of 89% and specificity of 94%.

Symptom frequency, duration, and severity are equally distributed among patients with varying grades of erosive esophagitis and Barrett's esophagus and cannot be used reliably to diagnose complications of GERD.
Physical examination is neither sensitive nor specific in diagnosing GERD or its complications.

Approximately 10% of hoarseness, up to 60% of chronic laryngitis and refractory sore throat, and 25% to 50% of globus sensation may be due to reflux; esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) and pH monitoring are frequently normal in this population.
About one-third of patients will have "disruptive" GERD, that is, frequent and/or severe symptoms.

Suspect eosinophilic esophagitis (EE) in patients with difficulty swallowing food or saliva, recurrent choking, belching or regurgitation, and other obstructive symptoms. Patients often have a history of asthma, allergies, eczema or other atopic disease. Symptoms may also increase seasonally with higher pollen counts.

The IMPACT acronym can be helpful when taking a history: Imbibing fluids with meals (to lubricate) Modifying food (cutting it into small pieces) Prolonged meal times Avoiding hard textured foods Chewing excessively Turning away pills
Patients who experience food bolus obstruction should undergo urgent endoscopy to look for stricture and other sources of obstruction.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD): the gold standard in assessing esophageal complications of GERD (eg, erosive esophagitis and Barrett's esophagus), but lacks an appreciable sensitivity and specificity for identifying pathologic reflux. It is recommended as part of initial evaluation in any patient with alarm symptoms (), over age 50, or with prolonged symptoms after a trial of medical therapy.
Validated clinical prediction rules to predict the risk of BE include the validated M-BERET and HUNT clinical prediction rules; the hyperlinks take you to those external calculators.
Consider an evaluation for heart disease in patients presenting with chest discomfort initially suspected to be due to GERD.

The 24-hour pH probe: accepted as the standard for establishing or excluding the presence of GERD, but is often inconvenient to the patient, and lacks the sensitivity and specificity (70%-96%) required to be a gold standard; more often used in infants and children to diagnose GERD. ACG guidelines (2022) recommend esophageal impedance-pH monitoring performed while the patient is taking a PPIs in patients whose GERD symptoms persist despite twice-daily PPI therapy.

Double-contrast Barium radiography has limited usefulness in making an accurate diagnosis of GERD, but may be useful in defining the presence of anatomic abnormalities, such as pyloric stenosis, malrotation and annular pancreas in the vomiting infant, as well as hiatal hernia and esophageal strictures in children and adults. It is not recommended routinely by ACG guidelines (2022).

High-resolution manometry (HRM) is not indicated for the diagnosis of GERD but can detect physiological abnormalities associated with GERD, such as low esophagogastric junction (EGJ) contractile index, hiatus hernia or weak peristalsis.

The Bernstein test: a test infusion into the distal esophagus of either 0.1N HCl or 0.9% NaCl in a single-blinded fashion with an assessment of the patient's response can be used to detect GERD, if a patient's symptoms are directly related to acid reflux (not widely used).
The diagnosis is confirmed by esophageal biopsies showing eosinophil-predominant inflammation, with at least 15 eosinophils per HPF or > 60 per mm2.
Many patients with EE have a normal appearing esophagus (about a quarter).

The probability that a patient with suspected GERD will respond to a PPI is related to their symptoms and body mass index (BMI). A validated clinical decision rule has been developed to predict response.
Validated diagnostic screening tools have been developed by Zimmerman and Manterola, although they are somewhat cumbersome for bedside use.

A clinical rule found that an initial length of involved esophagus of more than 6 cm and the presence of dysplasia predicts the likelihood of progression in patients with Barrett's esophagus. Patients with less than 6 cm involvement of Barrett's esophagus and no dysplasia have a 2.4% risk of any progression over 6 years.
Validated clinical prediction rules to predict the risk of BE include the validated M-BERET and HUNT clinical prediction rules; the hyperlinks take you to those external calculators
A diagnostic approach is outlined in .

Of patients who present with typical reflux symptoms, 70% will actually have GERD, so therapy is warranted. Lack of response to early treatment does not rule out GERD; a 2-week trial to determine the response to a PPI will not identify a significant proportion of patients who have true GERD.

Endoscopic screening for esophageal adenocarcinoma or Barrett's esophagus in patients with GERD is recommended for patients with alarm symptoms (), those over age 50, and those with prolonged symptoms. Otherwise initial endoscopy does not improve outcomes.

Asthma, Atopic Dermatitis, Anxiety and Depression and GERD are common conditions that often coexist. Mendelian Randomisation Analyisis suggests their complex genetic interplay. 50% to 80% of asthmatics have GERD and up to 75% have abnormal pH testing; however, only 30% of patients who have both GERD and asthma will have GERD as the cause for their asthma.

The role of GERD in the development of various cancers has been increasingly recognized, although direct causal relationships have yet to be definitively established. GERD is associated with an increased risk of lung, oral, throat, and esophageal cancers.

The risk of cancer is low in patients with Barrett's esophagus. The risk of cancer is approximately 0.12% to 0.24% per year in patients with BE. The need for endoscopic surveillance of patients with known Barrett's esophagus is not clear, but more studies are needed on this topic to define high-risk groups and surveillance intervals better. Closer surveillance is recommended for patients with BE and dysplasia.

Treatment with H2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs) and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) provide greater symptomatic relief and healing of erosive esophagitis as compared with placebo; PPIs are superior to H2RAs, but there is no difference between PPIs regarding their therapeutic efficacy. Vonoprazan may be superior to lansoprazole for treatment of severe erosive esophagitis.A
A PPI is recommended for acute and maintenance therapy for patients with documented erosive esophagitis.A
Carafate and antacids are less effective but may be used as supplemental acid-neutralizing agents for certain patients with GERD. C

On-demand (patient-directed) therapy for GERD is effective in uninvestigated reflux disease, nonerosive reflux disease, and possibly mild esophagitis as well and should not be considered for patients with severe esophagitis. B

In real-world settings, both continuous and on-demand PPI prescriptions resulted in similar increases in PPI consumption with no difference in treatment effects. Achieving an adequate PPI dose to alleviate reflux symptom burden improves quality of life in GERD patients.
Lifestyle modifications should be recommended for treatment of GERD and may be effective, especially in patients with mild or moderate symptoms (). C

For eosinophilic esophagitis: consider PPI twice daily, inhaled budesonide or other topical delivery, and six food elimination diet (cow’s milk, wheat, egg, soy, peanuts/tree nuts, fish and seafood) with dupilumab as a second line option.C
An approach to therapy is outlined in .

For patients with typical GERD symptoms and no alarm symptoms (weight loss, bleeding, dysphagia) ACG guidelines (2022) recommend an initial 8 week trial of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI). An attempt to discontinue proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) should then take place. If unsuccessful, consider diagnostic endoscopy 2 to 4 weeks after discontinuation of PPIs.
A PPI given 30 to 60 minutes before a meal is recommended over bedtime administration. PPIs are also recommended over H2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs).

For patients without erosive esophagitis or Barrett's esophagus, trials of discontinuing or weaning the PPI should be attempted. A study of 73 older patients taking a PPI found that about half could be tapered successfully to an H2RA or no medicine at all.

A meta-analysis demonstrated that H2RAs taken in divided doses twice daily are approximately 75% effective in treating patients with mild-to- moderate esophagitis and approximately 50% effective in treating patients with moderate to severe esophagitis. The effectiveness of H2RAs was confirmed by a Cochrane review.32 However, a Cochrane review concluded that PPIs are superior to H2RAs in head to head trials.
PPI treatment does not improve persistent throat symptoms.
ACG guidelines recommend sucralfate only in pregnancy.

PPIs are associated with uncommon but important potential harms with long-term use. The use of PPIs is associated with a small absolute increase (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.33 to 2.0) in the absolute risk of gastric cancer. There is a small increase in the risk of community-acquired pneumonia (NNH 449/y), with a higher risk in patients taking high or twice daily doses of a PPI. There is also an increased risk of hip fracture in patients taking long-term high-dose PPIs (odds ratio 2.65).
A meta-analysis of RCTs found no association between PPIs and cardiovascular events, though.

Potassium-competitive acid blockers (PCABs) such as vonoprazan have similar efficacy to PPI in non-erosive GERD and could be helpful in patients with severe erosive esophagitis (EE), and in the management of PPI-refractory GERD.

A systematic review with meta-analysis from four studies of adults with healed EE found that the potassium-competitive acid blocker (PCAB) vonoprazan 10 and 20 mg is superior to lansoprazole 15 mg in the maintenance of the healing of EE.
Eosinphilic esophagitis (EoE)

Standard therapy includes twice daily PPI are first line, with topical steroids an option for non-responders. Topical steroids include as an inhaler (fluticasone), as a budesonide slurry, and as orodispersable tablets.
Dupilumab is effective but is second line. An RCT comparing dupilumab with placebo in 102 children 1 to 11 years with EoE found histologic improvements with limited data on symptomatic relief.

Another RCT compared dupilumab with placebo in 81 adults with EoE and found greater likelihood of histologic resolution (60% vs 5%) and a greater reduction in an 85 point symptom score (-22 vs -10 points, p < .001).

Agents that are not recommended: montelukast, anti-histamines, sodium cromoglycate, systemic steroids, azathioprine, 6 mercaptopurine, and monoclonal antibodies developed for inflammatory bowel disease.

For patients with severe reflux esophagitis, large hiatal hernias, or persistent GERD symptoms despite adequate medical therapy, ACG guidelines (2022) recommend consideration of anti-reflux surgery in an experienced center.
For patients with severe esophagitis, symptoms scores 1 year after surgery are better than with medical treatment.

Patients assigned to medical management have lower mortality rates and an equal quality of life compared with patients undergoing surgical treatment. After 10 years of follow-up postsurgery, 92% of the medically and 62% of the surgically treated patients reported that they were still using acid suppressive medications on a regular basis.
Radiofrequency energy application to the distal esophagus (Stretta procedure) produces modest benefits over a sham procedure in the treatment of GERD.

The RefluxStop device is an implant placed via laparoscopic surgery in the stomach to mimic normal function of the gastroesophageal junction. It was well tolerated and effective in a small, uncontrolled case series of 50 patients.
Medical therapy is less expensive than surgical therapy for the treatment of GERD. The balance of benefits and harms comparing surgery to medical management is unclear.
In patients that respond to PPI therapy, continued therapy with PPI is modestly superior to (NNT 11-14) laparascopic antireflux surgery.
Patients with significant stricture or obstructive symptoms may benefit from dilation.

Lifestyle measures recommended by ACG guidelines include weight loss in obese patients, avoiding meals within 2 to 3 hours of bedtime, not smoking, elevating the head of bed for nighttime symptoms, and avoiding foods that trigger symptoms.

For patients with persistent reflux symptoms, consider comorbid anxiety and depression. A study in 393 adults with refractor heartburn found that general psychological functioning was significantly associated with overall reflux symptoms, heartburn, and sleep disturbances. General symptoms (e.g., depressive and various anxiety symptoms) were also associated with overall reflux symptoms and sleep disturbances, with visceral anxiety associated with heartburn severity.
Eosinophilic esophagitis
In patients with eosinophilic esophagitis, a food elimination program in consultation with a dietician can be attempted.
Elimination and stepwise reiintroduction of six foods is recommended: cow’s milk, wheat, egg, soy, peanuts/tree nuts, fish and seafood.
Referral to a gastroenterologist is warranted if a patient exhibits any of the alarm symptoms associated with GERD (), presents with prolonged or severe symptoms, or is over age 50 when they present.
Complications include Barrett's esophagus (10%), esophageal stricture (about 5%), esophageal ulcer (about 3%), hemorrhage, and perforation (rare).
Esophageal stricture can be managed with esophageal dilatation and chronic PPI therapy while esophageal ulcers are best healed with PPI therapy compared with H2RAs.
Many patients with symptomatic lower esophageal stricture will require more than one dilation to relieve symptoms.

Esophageal adenocarcinoma is the most ominous complication and is seen in approximately 0.5% of patients per year who have more than 3 cm of Barrett's esophagus and specialized intestinal metaplasia; it occurs in 0.07% in those who do not have Barrett's esophagus.
Antireflux surgery may be superior to medical therapy to prevent esophageal adenocarcinoma. This difference is more pronounced in patients with Barrett's.
Management of Barrett's esophagus and esophageal cancer is discussed elsewhere.
Eosinophilic esophagitis is a common cause of spontaneous perforation of the esophagus and can occur at any age.
Chronic reflux has been suspected to play a major role in the development of Barrett's esophagus, yet it is unknown whether outcomes can be improved through surveillance and medical treatment. C
If a patient with GERD symptomatology has an unremarkable EGD, then a follow-up endoscopy is not needed for 10 years in the absence of any alarm symptoms. B

GERD is a spectrum of disease states ranging from mild, intermittent symptoms of heartburn and acid regurgitation (nonerosive esophagitis/nonerosive reflux disease), to erosive esophagitis, to severe cases leading to the development of esophageal strictures, Barrett's esophagus, and potentially adenocarcinoma of the esophagus.

In patients seeking medical attention, most will have chronic symptoms that occur off treatment. Patients with more severe esophagitis will have symptoms recur more quickly, and almost all will have recurrent symptoms and esophagitis if followed up for longer than 1 year.
Progression of disease can be seen in up to 25% of patients with esophagitis, but it is less likely to occur if esophagitis is not present or is mild.
A population-based study in Sweden found Barrett's esophagus in 2.3% of patients with reflux symptoms and 1.2% without reflux.

Complications such as Barrett's esophagus, esophageal ulcers, esophageal stricture, or adenocarcinoma of the esophagus are very rare unless the initial endoscopy shows esophagitis or Barrett's esophagus.
Esophageal cancer risk is not increased in patients with non-erosive GERD. Erosive GERD increases the risk of esophageal cancer, but the risk is still low.
A normal upper endoscopy in the presence of GERD symptomatology represents a good prognosis.
In patients who undergo routine upper endoscopy, approximately 1% to 2% will have Barrett's esophagus.
The prevalence of Barrett's esophagus in patients with erosive esophagitis is approximately 10%; in patients with peptic strictures of the esophagus, the prevalence is almost 30%.
The best approach to detection and management of Barrett's esophagus is unclear. Referral should not be considered unless a patient is high risk (men over age 60 with prolonged or severe GERD).
Psychology factors are important in patients with refractory GERD symptoms and may be more important than physiological factors.
Females, despite comprising the majority hospitalized patients with GERD, had a lower incidence of GERD related complications.
There are no current evidence-based guidelines to direct patient follow-up for GERD symptom in the absence of alarm or extraesophageal symptoms.
Repeat endoscopy is not recommended for at least 10 years in patients whose symptoms remain unchanged.

Further diagnostic testing (eg, EGD, pH monitoring) should be considered in patients who do not respond to prolonged acid suppression therapy and in patients with a chronic history of GERD who are at risk for complications (eg, Barrett's esophagus, adenocarcinoma, stricture).
Chronic reflux has been suspected to play a role in the development of Barrett's esophagus, yet it is unknown whether outcomes can be improved through surveillance and medical treatment.
Lifestyle modifications should be recommended in conjunction with pharmacotherapy ().
Patients should consult their physician in the event of any alarm symptoms or any warning signs suggesting complicated GERD.
GERD is more common in pregnant women than in the general population.
Treatment options include over-the counter antacids, H2RAs, and secondarily PPIs.

Gastroesophageal reflux symptoms are common, occurring daily in approximately 40% of infants, with 25% of infants spitting up more than four times per day. Symptoms often begin before 8 weeks of life, peak at approximately 4 months of age, and usually resolve by 1 year. The prevalence of gastroesophageal reflux is 2% to 8% in children and adolescents

Diagnostic evaluation is indicated if there are signs of poor weight gain, GI obstruction, excessive crying and irritability, disturbed sleep, or feeding or respiratory problems suggesting suspected asthma or recurrent pneumonia.

European guidelines recommend (in the absence of alarm symptoms) dietary changes but no PPI for infants. In older children lifestyle and dietary changes are recommended as initial therapy, followed by short-term acid suppression therapy for 1 to 2 months if that is not effective. If symptoms persist after stopping acid suppression, referral to a pediatric gastroenterologist should be considered.
In children and adolescents, the use of PPIs was effective in achieving histological remission in patients with erosive esophagitis, accompanied by an improvement in symptoms.
In infants data from RCTs does not support the use of PPIs in reducing the symptoms related to GERD, including crying and irritability in infants.
In bottle fed babies thickened formula may reduce regurgitation by 2 episodes per day.
A trial of time-limited acid-suppression therapy, usually with H2RAs, is useful in determining whether GERD is causing vomiting and regurgitation.
In infants and children there is insufficient evidence to support the safety and efficacy of H2RAs.
In children long-term (eg, 3 years) use of PPIs appears to be safe.

feature.feature_body: Anorexia Chronic cough Choking Dysphagia Gastrointestinal bleed Hoarseness Iron deficiency anaemia Odynophagia Weight loss Adapted from Sandhu DS, Fass R. Current trends in the management of gastroesophageal reflux disease. Gut Liver 2018;12(1):7–16. doi: 10.5009/gnl16615 and

feature.caption: Lifestyle Modifications Suggested for the Treatment of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) Include.
feature.feature_body: Raising head end of the bed Avoiding meals within 3 hours of bedtime Weight loss Avoiding medications that may make symptoms worse calcium channel blockers, Beta agonists, alpha adrenergic agonists, theophylline, Nitrates, sedatives bisphosphonates, corticosteroids non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs] Avoiding foods or habits that may make symptoms worse e.g. tobacco, chocolate, carbonated beverages, onion, tomato sauce, mint, alcohol, citrus juices, spicy and fatty meals Recognising that psychological therapies, such as cognitive behavioural therapy and psychotherapy, may reduce dyspeptic symptoms in the short term in individual people. Adapted from Sandhu DS, Fass R. Current trends in the management of gastroesophageal reflux disease. Gut Liver 2018;12(1):7–16. doi: 10.5009/gnl16615 and
